questions.question: Explain the difference between fat soluble and water soluble vitamins with examples. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the difference between fat soluble and water soluble vitamins with
  • examples.
  • Vitamins are classified into fat-soluble vitamins and water-soluble vitamins based
  • on solubility.
  • Fat Soluble Vitamins:
  • - Include Vit. A, D, E, K
  • - Are usually found in fat rich foods and accumulate in body gradually.
  • - Doesn’t have nitrogen in its chemical structure.
  • - Are mostly heat stable.
  • - Absorbed indirectly by intestine along with dietary fats and lipids.
  • Water Soluble Vitamins:
  • - Include Vit. C and B complex
  • - They do not accumulate in body as excess is excreted via kidneys.
  • - B complex has nitrogen in its chemical structure.
  • - Are less heat stability.
  • - Absorbed directly into bloodstream.

questions.question: Why are microbial sources preferred for clean label products and large scale industrial applications? / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Why are microbial sources preferred for clean label products and large scale
  • industrial applications?
  • Microbial sources are preferred for clean label products and large -scale industrial
  • applications because they offer sustainable, consistent, and efficient production of
  • bioactive compounds without relying on synthetic chemicals or animal -derived
  • inputs. Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeast, and fungi can be cultivated rapidly in
  • controlled environments, ensuring reproducibility, scalability, and cost-effectiveness.
  • They naturally produce enzymes, vitamins, organic acids, and biofertilizers that align
  • with consumer demand for minimally processed, eco -friendly, and safe products.
  • Additionally, microbial processes reduce environmental impact by lowering resource
  • consumption and waste generation, making them ideal for industries seeking both
  • clean label compliance and industrial efficiency.

questions.question: Explain the importance of carbohydrates in human nutrition. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain the importance of carbohydrates in human nutrition.
  • Carbohydrates are the main energy -giving macronutrients composed of carbon,
  • hydrogen and oxygen. They are the most important and readily available source of
  • energy in the human diet.
  • Carbohydrates provide about 4 kcal/g of energy and act as the primary fuel for brain
  • and muscle activities. They are the precursors of many fats and amino acids. They
  • store excess energy as glycogen in liver and muscles to meet immediate energy
  • demand of the body. Carbohydrates spare proteins from being used for energy and
  • help in proper fat metabolism and prevent ketosis. They improve digestion through
  • dietary fibre, maintain normal blood glucose level and support overall metabolic
  • activities of the body.

questions.question: Explain food adulteration and its impact on human health. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Explain food adulteration and its impact on human health.
  • Food adulteration is the purposeful addition of substances that are foreign, inferior,
  • harmful and unauthorized, to food or removal of valuable components from food to
  • attain unfair profit. This is usually done for various reasons: to gain more profit,
  • increase shelf life, boost volume, improve appearance, enhance taste, and other
  • properties. (1 mark)
  • Impact on Human Health: (4 marks)
  • Acute Toxicity & Gastrointestinal Issues: Adulterants like contaminated water in milk
  • or chemical additions can cause immediate vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, and
  • severe food poisoning.
  • Organ Damage & Chronic Toxicity: Long -term consumption of toxic adulterants
  • places a heavy burden on the liver and kidneys (the primary detoxifying organs),
  • leading to liver cirrhosis, kidney stones, or renal failure. For instance, argemone oil
  • in mustard oil causes epidemic dropsy and cardiac failure.
  • Carcinogenic Risks: Non -permitted synthetic food colors (e.g., metanil yellow in
  • turmeric) and industrial dyes are highly carcinogenic and can lead to various types of
  • cancers.
  • Nutritional Deficiencies: Diluting essential foods (like adding water to milk or starch
  • to ghee) reduces the bioavailability of essential macro and micronutrients, leading to
  • malnutrition, especially in children. (Any four impacts)

questions.question: Define lipids. Classify fatty acids into saturated and unsaturated fatty acids with examples and functions. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Define lipids. Classify fatty acids into saturated and unsaturated fatty acids
  • with examples and functions.
  • Lipids are a group of hydrophobic (water -insoluble) organic compounds mainly
  • composed of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. They include fats, oils, waxes,
  • phospholipids and sterols. Lipids provide a concentrated source of energy, act as
  • structural components of cell membranes, provide insulation and protection to
  • organs and serve as precursors of hormones. (2 marks)
  • Fatty acids are long chain carboxylic acids that form the basic building blocks of
  • lipids.
  • Classification of fatty acids
  • Saturated fatty acids: Saturated fatty acids contain only single bonds between
  • carbon atoms so they are fully saturated with hydrogen atoms. They are generally
  • solid at room temperature. Major sources are animal fats like butter, ghee, meat fat
  • and plant oils such as coconut oil and palm oil. They mainly provide energy storage
  • and structural roles, but excess intake may increase cholesterol levels. Examples
  • include palmitic acid and stearic acid. (4 marks)
  • Unsaturated fatty acids: Unsaturated fatty acids contain one or more double bonds
  • in their carbon chain, making them less saturated with hydrogen. They are usually
  • liquid at room temperature. Major sources are vegetable oils (sunflower, olive,
  • soybean oil), nuts, seeds, and fish oils. They help in maintaining membrane fluidity,
  • reducing cholesterol levels, supporting brain and nerve function and acting as
  • essential fatty acids in the diet. Examples include oleic acid, linoleic acid, and
  • linolenic acid. (4 marks)

questions.question: Describe high-temperature preservation methods used in food processing. / [CO3] [10x1 = 10]
questions.solution_html:
• Describe high-temperature preservation methods used in food processing.
  • High temperature preservation is a method of food preservation in which heat is
  • applied to destroy microorganisms and inactivate enzymes responsible for food
  • spoilage. Heat causes proteins and metabolic enzymes of microorganisms to
  • coagulate, thereby preventing their growth and extending the shelf life of foods. The
  • effectiveness of heat treatment depends on the type of microorganism present, the
  • nature of the food, and the preservation method used. (Definition 2 Marks)
